opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that I don't think we have a great answer yet, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claims to. But I can say how I think about the shape of the problem.

AI matters here in two ways. It may make existing destructive capabilities, like bioweapons or cyberattacks, much cheaper and more accessible. And it may create new kinds of risk, including AI systems that are themselves dangerous because we can't reliably control them. Those call for somewhat different responses.

For the first category, I think the natural model is something like existing nonproliferation regimes, but with a lot more emphasis on verification at the level of capabilities rather than intentions. Historically, international agreements work when you can check compliance. With nuclear weapons, you can monitor fissile material and big facilities. With AI, the analogous chokepoints are probably compute, the large training runs and the chips and data centers that make them possible, and maybe evaluations of what models can actually do before they're deployed. So I'd like agreements that say, roughly: if your system crosses certain capability thresholds, say it can meaningfully help someone build a biological weapon, then you need certain safeguards, and other parties can get some assurance you've implemented them.

The second category is harder, because the danger isn't just bad actors misusing a tool. It's that everyone, including well-intentioned developers, may be racing to build systems they don't fully understand. There I think the most valuable thing an agreement can do is reduce the pressure to cut corners. If labs or countries believe that slowing down to do safety work means losing to a competitor, they'll slow down less than they should. A credible agreement, even a fairly modest one, that says "nobody deploys systems past this level until we can demonstrate they're safe in these specific ways" changes that calculus.

I'd also stress something I've talked about in the context of responsible scaling policies: you want commitments that are conditional. It's very hard to get countries to agree to stop doing something today based on speculative risks. It's much easier to agree that if we observe some specific warning sign, then we'll do X. That lets people who are skeptical of the risks sign on, because they think the condition won't trigger, while giving real protection if the people worried about it turn out to be right.

And finally, I think we should be realistic. International coordination is slow, and AI is moving fast. So a lot of the near-term work is building the infrastructure, the evaluations, the measurement science, the channels of communication between governments, so that when the political will shows up, often after some scary event, there's something concrete ready to adopt rather than people scrambling to figure it out from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response mentions new AI-related risks and says AI is moving fast, but it does not identify the rapid emergence of many new kinds of harm as AI’s key role in the problem.

r002.rationale: It proposes AI-focused agreements based on shared capability thresholds, compute, training runs, and model evaluations, rather than treating each physical technology as a separate target.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where I want to separate out a few different things, because I think people often run them together.

The first thing is that I don't think the right frame is mostly "AI creates new destructive technologies and we need to regulate those technologies." I think the right frame is closer to: AI is going to dramatically accelerate the rate at which we discover and can deploy all kinds of technologies, some of which are destructive, and the institutions we have for handling that are built for a world where that rate is slow. So the Biological Weapons Convention, the nuclear nonproliferation regime, these things took decades to negotiate and they're premised on the idea that the relevant capabilities are scarce, expensive, and attributable. If you can detect that someone's enriching uranium, you have time to react. A lot of what worries me about AI is that it compresses that timeline and potentially makes the relevant capabilities much cheaper and more diffuse.

So one thing I'd say is that agreements probably shouldn't be organized primarily around specific downstream technologies, because by the time you've identified the technology and negotiated something, you're behind. I think they have to be organized at least partly around the AI systems themselves, and in particular around compute, because that's the input that's actually legible and controllable right now. You can count chips. You can know where the big data centers are. That's a very unusual property for a dangerous technology to have and I think we should take advantage of it while it lasts, because I don't think it lasts forever.

The second thing I'd say is that I think the most important function of an international agreement in this area isn't actually prohibiting any particular thing. It's creating the ability to slow down or pause if we collectively decide we need to. Right now, if the US and China both became convinced tomorrow that frontier development was too dangerous, there's no mechanism by which they could credibly verify that the other side is also stopping. And so the rational thing for each of them to do is keep going. I think a lot of the value of agreements is just building that verification capacity in advance, so that the option to coordinate exists when you need it. That looks like: monitoring of large training runs, agreed reporting on compute, some kind of inspection regime for the biggest facilities. None of that requires agreeing right now on what the limits should be. It just requires agreeing that we want to be able to set limits later.

Third, on the destructive technologies specifically, like biology, I do think there's a role for more conventional agreements, and I'd be pretty supportive of them. Things like norms around what capabilities frontier models are allowed to have, shared evaluations for dangerous capabilities, obligations to not deploy systems that meaningfully uplift someone trying to build a bioweapon. I'm somewhat more optimistic about this in the bio case than people might expect, because I think there's actually a lot of shared interest. Nobody wants a world where a random individual can synthesize a pandemic pathogen, including the governments that are otherwise competing with each other. So I think the bio stuff is in some ways the easy case, and the hard case is the stuff that's dual-use in the military sense, where one country's safety measure is another country's disadvantage.

And then the last thing I'd say, and this is maybe the most uncomfortable one, is that I think we should be honest that a lot of these agreements will be fairly weak initially and that's okay. The history of arms control is mostly a history of agreements that were imperfect, that were partially violated, that were renegotiated, but that still shifted the equilibrium and bought time. I think the goal for the next few years is less "get the right treaty" and more "build the relationships, the technical capacity, and the shared understanding so that when it becomes clear that something needs to be done, it's possible to do it." I'm much more worried about a world where we've done none of that groundwork than a world where we've negotiated a treaty with the wrong thresholds.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will dramatically accelerate the discovery and deployment of many technologies, some destructive, while making dangerous capabilities cheaper and more diffuse.

r002.rationale: It argues agreements should not focus mainly on specific downstream technologies and should instead address AI systems, including compute.

astra-6.text:
I think you want agreements that are relatively robust to uncertainty about what the technology looks like. We don’t know exactly which destructive capabilities AI will enable, so a treaty that’s just a list of things we already know how to build seems pretty inadequate.

One approach is to focus on the process by which those capabilities get developed. Before you build or deploy a sufficiently powerful AI system, you need some way to assess whether it would enable a small group to cause catastrophic damage, and safeguards if it would. International agreements could establish common standards for those assessments and some verification that countries are actually following them.

The hard part is that everyone also has a legitimate interest in benefiting from AI, and often the same capabilities have both beneficial and destructive applications. So you’d like the restrictions to be targeted, but you also need a mechanism for updating them as you learn more.

I think verification is particularly important. It’s much easier to agree that no one should do something dangerous than to create a situation where each country can be confident that the others aren’t doing it. And if you can’t establish that confidence, even countries that would prefer mutual restraint may feel compelled to race.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI may enable unknown destructive capabilities, but does not identify the rapid emergence of many new kinds of harm as AI’s key role.

r002.rationale: It proposes agreements focused on assessing and safeguarding sufficiently powerful AI systems, rather than listing or regulating each physical technology separately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between restricting access to a dangerous technology and making the world robust to it. If AI makes it much easier to build a biological weapon, for example, you probably want some restrictions on assistance with that. But you also want to use AI to improve detection, develop countermeasures, and make an attack less likely to succeed.

International agreements can help with both. Countries could agree on what kinds of assistance AI systems shouldn’t provide, how to test whether those restrictions actually work, and what information to share when someone discovers a new vulnerability. You’d also want commitments to defensive research, because restrictions alone become much less reassuring as the technology spreads.

The hard question is verification. An agreement that says, ‘Nobody will do dangerous things with AI’ doesn’t accomplish much if you can’t tell whether anyone is complying. So I’d start with narrower commitments where you can establish some observable evidence of compliance, then expand those as we learn more about the risks and the available defenses. I wouldn’t expect one grand agreement to settle all of this in advance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI making biological weapons easier to build, but does not identify the rapid emergence of many new kinds of harm as AI’s key role.

r002.rationale: It proposes agreements on what assistance AI systems should not provide, a broad AI-focused commitment that can apply across technologies.
